scenarios.description: A started job runs on its own: its combined output is readable from offset 0, and it ends with the shell's exit code.
start answers with the job's process group, which leads a group of its own.

read returns up to max bytes from offset, reports where the data starts (offset) and where the job's output ends so far (end, the same whatever max was), and an offset at the end is empty with the job's final state.
Output is readable while the job still runs, and state says running with no code.
The job's status is the shell's exit code.
A job killed by signal N has status 128+N.

A job whose shell cannot find its command ends with 127. (Starting a program that does not exist at all is refused by the endpoint with an error status: callers wrap commands in sh -c to get one behaviour.)
stdout and stderr are one combined output, in the order the bytes were written (best effort between the two).
Job output is bytes: all 256 values come back exactly.

args: i=0; while [ $i -lt 256 ]; do printf "\\$(printf %03o $i)"; i=$((i+1)); done

scenarios.description: A job's stdin is empty: cat ends at once.
cwd and argv are as for exec: arguments arrive verbatim.
list shows the scope's jobs with id, state, code, kept, label and start time; a running job has no code.
list returns every job of the scope, ended ones until removed.
kill signals the job's whole process group: a child it started dies too.
A job that ignores SIGTERM is killed anyway after the grace: kill returns when the group is empty.

args: trap '' TERM; echo ready; while :; do sleep 1; done

scenarios.description: Killing a job that already ended signals nothing and succeeds.
kill with remove deletes the job once its group is gone: it is then gone, and no longer listed.
Killing a job that does not exist is not an error.
remove deletes ended jobs and never a running one.
remove is idempotent.
Reading a job that never existed is state gone with no data, not an error.
Scopes are separate namespaces: the same id in another scope is another job, and one scope cannot list, read, kill or remove another's.
wipe kills every job of the scope and deletes them all.
attach streams a job's output from an offset to its end and reports its status; on an ended job that is what is left, at once.
attach on a running job follows its output until it ends.

args: echo a; sleep 0.5; echo b; exit 3

scenarios.description: attach reports a signalled job as `signal` N, not an exit code.
A quarter megabyte of output follows through whole.

When the shell exits leaving a background process in its group, the job is 'exited' (with the shell's code) until the group is empty, then 'ended' with the same code. The leftover lives until the scenario kills it, so 'exited' lasts as long as the poll needs.
attach does not end at the shell's exit but when the group is empty; the status is the shell's.
A job id is 1 to 32 characters of [0-9a-z]; anything else is refused before any request is sent.
An id is unique within its scope: starting it again while it exists is an error and leaves the first job alone.
At least the last 8 MiB of a job's output is kept; older output is dropped as a gap of known size, and offsets never move.
A job whose shell is killed by signal S reports `signal` S beside `code` 128 + S, in read and in list, as a stream's signal frame does.
A job that exits 137 by itself reports `code` 137 and no `signal`: an exit of 128 + S is not told from a signal by the number.
A job stopped with kill reports the signal it was killed with: 15, or 9 when it ignored the grace period.
Attaching to a job whose shell a signal killed ends as a stream does: `signal` in place of `exit_code`.
Attaching to a job that exited 137 by itself ends with `exit_code` 137 and no `signal`.
A job's stderr bytes are named on the output's own offsets: read answers stderr_ranges, and the combined data is unchanged.

args: printf AAA; sleep 0.3; printf BBB >&2; sleep 0.3; printf CCC

scenarios.description: A window with no stderr carries no stderr_ranges.
An attach keys each output frame by its pipe; the combined output is unchanged.

args: printf AAA; sleep 0.3; printf BBB >&2; sleep 0.3; printf CCC

scenarios.description: A one-shot command runs with the env it was given, values exact.
A job runs with the env it was started with.
A name starting EXECD_ is refused and runs nothing.
Positional writes to an open stdin: a repeat applies nothing twice, an overlap applies its new suffix, EOF ends cat.
A job started without stdin_open has no stdin to write.
A write to no job is not_found.
signal reaches the job's group once; an ended job is not signalled; SIGKILL reads as signal 9.

args: trap 'printf I' INT; trap 'printf U' USR1; printf ready; while :; do (trap '' INT USR1; sleep 0.2); done

scenarios.description: A signal off the list is invalid_request.
Attaching to a job that does not exist is a typed error, JobGone, which is a kind of not_found.
A read of a removed job says JobGone, as attach does. The wire's own answer is state `gone`, which a driver reports when it is not asked for the error.
Starting an id that exists is JobExists, a kind of conflict, and leaves the first job running.
A write to a job started without stdin_open is StdinClosed with reason never_opened, a kind of conflict.
A write after EOF is StdinClosed with reason closed: it is told apart from a stdin that never opened, and retrying cannot succeed.
A write to no job is JobGone, a kind of not_found.
keep names the job's number, kind and seen offset, and list reports them.
keep, and seen, of no job are JobGone.
seen records the offset of the output shown, and list reports it.
hold: true ties the job to the stream that started it: closing the stream before the job ends and before keep kills its group.
A held job that was kept before its stream closed keeps running: it is still there, and still writing, a moment after the stream is gone.

args: echo up; sleep 0.8; echo alive; sleep 60

scenarios.description: grace_ms is the time between SIGTERM and SIGKILL: a job that needs a second to wind down finishes cleanly with a long grace, and is killed with the default 300 ms.

args: trap 'sleep 1; echo clean; exit 0' TERM; echo ready; while :; do sleep 0.1; done
trap 'sleep 1; echo clean; exit 0' TERM; echo ready; while :; do sleep 0.1; done

scenarios.description: A request may choose its stream's heartbeat (Keepalive-Ping-Interval, whole seconds 1 to 240): the stream still delivers the job's output and end. Anything else is invalid_request, sent nowhere.
A job started with `pty` runs with a terminal on stdin, stdout and stderr at the size asked for, the start answer echoes the terminal, and `read` reports it.
The command's terminal is its controlling terminal: opening /dev/tty works.
A terminal merges stderr into its one output stream: both lines come as stdout with the terminal's CRLF, `read` names no stderr bytes and `attach` no stderr frames.
Input written to a terminal is echoed by the terminal and run by the shell.
Positional writes to a terminal land once: a repeat of the same bytes at the same position applies nothing, and the bytes are echoed by the terminal once and printed by the program once.
A resize changes the terminal's size and the program is told: it gets SIGWINCH and reads the new size.

args: trap "stty size" WINCH; echo ready; while :; do sleep 0.05; done

scenarios.description: A size outside 1 to 1024 is invalid_request and changes nothing; the same job then takes 1024 by 1024.
A resize of a job that is not there is not_found; of a job with no terminal, or of a terminal that has ended, conflict.
Writing 0x03 to a terminal is Ctrl-C: the terminal sends SIGINT to the foreground program.
A terminal has no end of input: `eof` is invalid_request and applies nothing; the same position still takes data, and 0x04 at the start of a line ends cat.
`signal` reaches the terminal's whole session: a shell and the program it runs both end.
A kept terminal outlives the stream that started it: a new connection lists it running with its terminal, writes to it, and attaches from the offset it had.
`list` shows a terminal job's size and that it is open; a job without a terminal has no `pty`.
After the terminal's job has ended, a write is conflict (it says how much was written) and so is a resize.
A terminal survives a restart of the endpoint's process: the shell is the same one, offsets continue, a write at the old position lands once, and its real exit code is reported.

A terminal survives a crash of the endpoint's process (SIGKILL, no shutdown at all, then a new process on the same URL): the shell is the same one, offsets continue, a write at the old position lands once, and its real exit code is reported.
A terminal whose keeper is killed is hung up, not lost: it reads closed, input and resize are conflict, `eof` is still the client's error, the job can still be killed, and a new terminal opens.

args: trap '' HUP; echo up; exec sleep 300
